newsitem.title: USA: U.S. claims fall shows strikes, floods skewed data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. claims fall shows strikes, floods skewed data.

text.p: It appears that jobless claims have come back to earth, and the labor market remains tight.
After two weeks of claims around the 350,000 level, the data released on Thursday put the number of initial filers back to where it was three weeks ago.
The U.S. Labor Department reported that jobless claims fell to 319,000 in the week ended May 10, from a revised 350,000 in the prior week.
Analysts said it was clear that strikes at automakers' plants and flooding in the Midwest had pushed the data upward.

The huge 31,000 drop in the latest week "tells you that the increase the last two weeks was not a fundamntal deterioration in the labor market," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
The strikes at automakers' plants have ended, while the flooding has stopped.
"As flood waters receded so too have claims," Resler said.
Yet economists said they had not expected the effects of strikes and floods to dissapear so soon, if indeed, that was the case.
"Either (they) dissipated quicker than we thought or the underlying strength of labor is very strong," said Ken Bercuson, head of reserach at SBC Warburg Government Securities Inc.
Bercuson said that it was possible the strike and flood effects have not been fully realized and that the fall in claims was largely because "demand for labor is very strong."
As such, he said there is no doubt in his mind that the Federal Reserve will raise rates at Tuesday's Federal Reserve policy-setting meeting.
"We are going to see a huge (May) payroll number and continued pressure on the unemployment rate," Bercuson said.

He declined to predict the two figures until after next week's claims data -- the survey week for the payroll report, but speculated that nonfarm jobs would be above 200,000, while the unemployment rate could dip below 4.9 percent.
Meanwhile, some analysts said they would be watching the continuing claims figures for further signs of labor market tighteness.
Continuing claims rose to 2.314 million in the May 3 week, up from 2.291 million the prior week.
Economists said the increase reflects the strikes and floods, adding that it would take another week or two to straighten out.
In the meantime, the Fed debate rages on.
Chase Securities Inc senior economist James Glassman said the decline in initial claims would not affect the Fed's decision on whether to tighten monetary policy further.

"(Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan's pretty much put his finger on what he's looking at: he wants to see a decrease in consumer spending. They already know the labor market's tight, but the unemployment rate is not carved in stone."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
